definition: Forming a united whole whose parts fit together or work well as one.
example: Though written years apart, the album's songs form a cohesive story about leaving home.
nuance: Cohesive stresses parts holding together as one; coherent stresses logical clarity, so a clear speaker is coherent, not cohesive.
prompt: A coach describes how her soccer team played in the championship final.
options: The cohesive team passed smoothly because every player trusted the others.
The cohesive team argued constantly, and each player ignored the others' calls.
The cohesive team wore jerseys so sticky that the ball clung to their chests.
The cohesive striker explained her winning goal in one clear, logical sentence.
reasons: Players who trust each other and move the ball as one show real unity.
Constant arguing and ignoring teammates describe a team that is falling apart.
Physical stickiness is what adhesive means; the word describes unity, not glue.
A clear, logical explanation is coherent; one person speaking well is not a unified group.

practice.prompt: An interior designer is furnishing a family's living room.
options: She chose a cohesive palette so the rugs, lamps, and curtains all matched.
She chose a cohesive mix of clashing styles that seemed to have nothing in common.
She chose a cohesive paste to keep the new wallpaper from peeling off.
She chose a cohesive sofa because it was the cheapest one in the catalog.
reasons: Colors that tie every piece of the room together create a unified whole.
Pieces with nothing in common clash; they do not come together as one.
A paste that makes paper stick is adhesive, which is a different word.
Price says nothing about whether the parts of a room fit together.
